analysis.one_liner: Lets workers at employers with 15 or more staff earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate's labor committee in February 2015, received no action there, and died when that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (seven days) a year. The time could be used for a worker's own illness, medical care, caring for a sick child or family member, or handling domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking situations. Very small employers could opt out of paid leave but would have to offer 56 hours of unpaid sick time instead. It was introduced by Senator Patty Murray with 34 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who currently have no paid sick time — the bill's findings say nearly 40 percent of the private-sector workforce lacks it, with the lowest earners least covered. It would also help victims of domestic violence who need time off for medical care or court, and parents who need to care for sick children without losing pay.

how_it_helps.text: Workers would earn at least 1 hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year unless the employer offers more.

The time could be used for a worker's own medical needs, to care for family members including domestic partners, or to seek medical attention, relocation, or legal help related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Employers would be barred from firing, disciplining, or retaliating against workers for using the leave, counting it against attendance policies, or interfering with its use.
Employers with fewer than 15 employees could opt out of paid leave, but would have to provide at least 56 hours of unpaid sick time per year.
The Secretary of Labor would have investigative and enforcement authority, and workers could sue for lost wages and attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would cover the wage cost of up to seven days of leave a year. The cost falls hardest on low-margin, high-turnover industries like retail, food service, and hospitality, where paid sick leave is least common. Small employers would bear the administrative burden of tracking unpaid leave.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a direct payroll cost for covered employers — up to 56 hours of paid leave per employee per year — which falls hardest on businesses with thin margins and many low-wage hourly workers.
Businesses with fewer than 15 employees could avoid paying, but their workers would only get unpaid leave, so the lowest-paid workers at the smallest firms get less protection.
Earned sick time does not have to be paid out when a worker leaves the job, and employers with existing leave policies sufficient to meet the requirements owe nothing additional.
Employers would face recordkeeping and notice-posting requirements, with civil fines up to $100 per willful posting violation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: the bill's own findings show that low-wage workers — 70 percent of the lowest-paid quartile — lack paid sick time, forcing people to work sick, send sick children to school, or lose income. The cost is genuine but modest relative to the benefit: a capped seven days a year, with exemptions for the smallest firms and full credit for employers that already offer comparable leave. The main honest objection is that the cost lands on the employers least able to absorb it, and some of it may show up as slower hiring or reduced other benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee from February 2015 until the Congress ended in January 2017, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate on February 12, 2015, joined by 20 original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral was the last recorded action.
The bill attracted 34 cosponsors — 32 Democrats and 2 independents — and no Republicans.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have borne the cost of providing paid sick leave — particularly low-wage service industries where such leave is least common — are better off because the bill never advanced. Workers who lack paid sick time lost the protection entirely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for leave

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act on February 12, 2015.

for.name: 34 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a hearing or committee vote; it remained in committee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and chairing the labor committee, the bill received no action after its referral.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (retail, food service, hospitality)
industries.note: These employers would have had to pay for up to seven days of leave per employee per year, and they employ most of the workers who currently lack paid sick time. Their interest in avoiding the cost runs directly against their workers gaining the leave.

They were exempt from paying for leave but would have had to provide 56 hours of unpaid sick time and track its use, an administrative cost. Their workers would have gotten less protection than workers at larger firms.

industries.industry: Employers with existing generous leave policies
industries.note: The bill states it does not diminish existing contracts or benefit plans and requires nothing additional from employers whose current paid leave already meets the requirements, so well-covered workplaces would be unaffected.
